sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent harnesses enable large language models to act through tools, observe the results, and iteratively work toward a task goal. Verification checks and revises agents' work to improve output quality. Yet there is limited guidance on how harnesses should organize this effort. We study verification as an axis of test-time scaling by examining when to intervene, who checks the work, and how checking leads to revision. Our framework spans four layers of the agent lifecycle: initial instructions, mid-turn reminders, completion gates, and independent review. We compare 17 designs across seven frontier coding models on Terminal-Bench (TB) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE), and introduce VisualBench for expert evaluation of visual and interactive artifacts. Initial instructions and execution-time reminders yield modest, model-dependent average gains on the coding benchmarks, without substantially increasing average output token use. Completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost. Independent review by a critic offers a more favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.9-9.5 percentage points on TB and 3.9-6.6 on SWE at 1.13-1.25 and 1.00-1.04 times baseline cost, respectively. On VisualBench, independent review achieves net preferences of 13.2-23.8 points over the baseline across its four designs, exceeding the evaluated L0-L2 designs. Additional review rounds or independent critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for verification design in agent harnesses and support independent review as a practical axis of test-time scaling.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) tackle long-horizon software engineering tasks, including resolving repository-level issues across large codebases (Yang et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026; Google, 2026). These agents run inside harnesses that let the model act through tools, observe the results, and iterate toward task goal (Yao et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024). Beyond exposing tools, the harness speciﬁes the agents instructions, controls intervention timing, and coordinates veriﬁcation before accepting its work (Bolin, 2026; Lopopolo, 2026). These choices allocate computation to checking and revising the agents work, making veriﬁcation an important part of harness design (Lopopolo, 2026). Prior work develops learned veriﬁers for selecting solutions (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2023), self-correction through critiques and reﬂections (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), and tool-assisted checks that return execution evidence for repair (Gou et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023a). In practice, veriﬁcation in agent harnesses is often shaped by engineering heuristics and iterative experience: Claude Code provides hooks for completion checks (Anthropic, 2026b), while Codex uses self-review and iteration (Lopopolo, 2026). Yet systematic evidence remains limited on how to design and scale veriﬁcation, when design improves performance, and whether its gains justify the additional computation. Without this guidance, current designs may be suboptimal for given model or task. In this paper, we study veriﬁcation as an axis of test-time scaling in agent harnesses. We organize the design space around three questions: when to intervene, who should check the work, and how ﬁndings should lead to revision. Following the agent lifecycle, L0: Initial instructions and L1: Execution-time reminders shape what the agent is told before and during execution to guide its This work was done during an internship at Alibaba Group. 1 own checking; L2: Completion gates reopen its work for self-checking; and L3: Independent review assigns separate critic to check the work and return ﬁndings for repair before it is accepted. This framework lets us compare prompting the agent to verify, extending its self-checking, and introducing an independent checking perspective. Within these layers, we vary message role, intervention timing, critic context, and review strategy, then scale independent review through additional rounds or critics. We compare 17 veriﬁcation designs on Terminal-Bench (TB) (Merrill et al., 2026) and SWE-bench Veriﬁed (SWE) (Jimenez et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2024) tasks using seven frontier coding models: Qwen3.7-Max (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026b), GLM-5.2 (Z.ai, 2026), DeepSeek V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), DeepSeek V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), Kimi-K2.7-Code (Moonshot AI, 2026), and MiniMax-M2.5 (MiniMax, 2026). We also introduce an internal VisualBench of 18 visual and interactive tasks, evaluated through blinded expert comparisons of functionality and visual quality. L0 initial instructions and L1 execution-time reminders yield modest, model-dependent average gains on the coding benchmarks, using 0.901.00 and 0.750.93 baseline output tokens, respectively. L2 completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost: rejection-based designs cost 1.601.76 baseline on TB and 1.48 1.56 on SWE. L3 independent review by separate critic offers more favorable accuracycost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.99.5 percentage points on TB and 3.96.6 on SWE at 1.131.25 and 1.001.04 baseline cost, respectively, including critic review and agent revision. On VisualBench, all four independent-review designs outperform the evaluated L0L2 designs, with net preferences of +13.2+23.8 points. Changes-based review outperforms trajectory-based review both with and without required visual inspection. Additional review rounds or independent critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for veriﬁcation design in agent harnesses and support independent review as practical axis of test-time scaling, enabling users to conﬁgure veriﬁcation effort for different tasks to improve agent performance.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Veriﬁcation. There is line of works exploring veriﬁcation for assessing candidates, guiding selfcorrection, and checking outputs against external evidence. Learned veriﬁers score complete solutions or intermediate reasoning steps to guide candidate selection (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a). Code-focused assessment ranges from trained critics that highlight bugs (McAleese et al., 2024) to review protocols that combine agent judgments or introduce structured disagreement (Tang et al., 2024; Qiu & Gill, 2026). Self-correction methods use naturallanguage critiques and reﬂections to revise outputs or improve subsequent attempts (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). Training-based approaches further teach models to improve across successive attempts through ﬁne-tuning or multi-turn reinforcement learning (Qu et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024). Studies of reasoning correction and code repair examine the limits of self-generated feedback and show that reported gains depend on feedback quality and the cost of additional attempts (Huang et al., 2023b; Olausson et al., 2023; Kamoi et al., 2024). Tool-assisted veriﬁcation grounds error detection in evidence from code execution and external tools (Chen et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2023), while dedicated test-generation and execution agents return test feedback to guide code revision (Huang et al., 2023a). Together, these strands provide the assessment and feedback mechanisms from which harness-level veriﬁcation designs can be built. Agent harnesses. Agent harnesses determine how models interact with tools and environments by organizing instructions, tool interfaces, execution ﬂow, and context. Prior work studies interleaved reasoning and action (Yao et al., 2022), agentcomputer interfaces (Yang et al., 2024), execution platforms (Wang et al., 2024b), and structured repair workﬂows (Xia et al., 2024). These studies examine how the surrounding execution design shapes agent behavior. Harness design also governs how computation and information are used across attempts, including agent sampling and selection (Zhu et al., 2025) and reuse of coding rollouts through structured summaries (Kim et al., 2026). Agent harnesses have become an essential part of modern coding agents, including Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a), Codex CLI (OpenAI, 2026), and Gemini CLI (Google, 2026). These works establish useful assessment mechanisms and agent workﬂows, but offer limited comparative guidance on how harness should organize checking and revision. sections.title: 3 VERIFICATION DESIGNS
sections.content: In this section, we introduce veriﬁcation designs by following the agent lifecycle, from receiving task to delivering result as shown in Figure 1. Table 1 summarizes when each layer intervenes, who checks the work, and how execution continues. Before execution begins, the agent receives the task and the instructions that guide its work. At this stage, L0: Initial instructions introduces veriﬁcation guidance into the initial prompt. We vary the message role of the veriﬁcation instructions: System or User. In the System variant, we append it to the system prompt as standing guidance. Because users do not always include veriﬁcation instructions in their requests, we introduce User variant that appends the same prompt to the initial user request. Both variants ask the agent to run the deliverable through its intended interface, inspect the output, and ﬁx observed defects. The L0 veriﬁcation instructions are in Appendix E.1. For visual or interactive artifacts, the instruction also asks the agent to render the result and exercise its core interactions. The L0 veriﬁcation instructions for visual tasks in our VisualBench are in Appendix E.1. As execution proceeds, changes to the codebase accumulate across turns. In our experiment, we ﬁnd that only 6.213.6% of detected editing turns are followed by recognized checking command 3 before the next editing turn or the end of the run, as reported in Appendix Table 7. We therefore introduce L1: Execution-time reminders to encourage the agent to check recent changes as it works, creating opportunities to identify and correct errors before further changes accumulate. These reminders arrive after tool results and before the next model call, so the agent can check its recent changes before continuing. We evaluate three designs. Periodic reminder (System) sends reminder few turns after the edit. After-edit reminder (System) sends the same reminder after turn that changes ﬁle. These two designs use marker identifying the message as an automated selfveriﬁcation checkpoint. After-edit reminder (User) uses the same edit-based trigger but delivers the reminder as user message without that marker. Thus, the ﬁrst comparison varies the trigger, while the second varies the message role and the presence of the automated marker. The L1 veriﬁcation instructions are in Appendix E.2. When the agent attempts to ﬁnish, L2: Completion gates reopen the agents work for checking and revision. To examine how the requested action guides subsequent checking and revision, we vary whether the gate asks the agent to inspect changes or run checks, or rejects completion and asks it to continue working. We vary the message role (System or User) and whether user messages carry an automated marker to study how these choices affect the agents response. We also vary intervention timing to test whether reserving time for checking and repair improves outcomes. The L2 prompts and triggering rules are in Appendix E.3. Before ﬁnal acceptance, the harness can also assign veriﬁcation to separate model, which we call the critic. This introduces L3: Independent review: the critic starts in fresh context and assesses the agents deliverable. The critic receives the task speciﬁcation and access to the live sandbox, where it can run its own checks. The critic returns its ﬁndings to the agent for revision. We vary the critics context and whether its checks are guided by task requirements alone (Task-ﬁrst) or also by the agents assumptions and claims (Claim-guided). The Changes condition provides the critic with the task and the agents changes. The Trajectory condition provides the task, changes, and the agents execution trajectory. The critic instructions are in Appendix E.4.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Models. We evaluate seven coding models through Alibaba Cloud Model Studio (DashScope): Qwen3.7-Max (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026b), GLM-5.2 (Z.ai, 2026), DeepSeek V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), DeepSeek V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), Kimi-K2.7-Code (Moonshot AI, 2026), and MiniMax-M2.5 (MiniMax, 2026). Qwen3.7-Plus serves as the independent critic for every coding model. Benchmarks. We evaluate on task subsets from Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB) (Merrill et al., 2026) and SWE-bench Veriﬁed (SWE) (Jimenez et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2024), both with automatic graders. Task selection aims to cover range of difﬁculties, using baseline success rates for TB and human time-to-ﬁx tiers followed by baseline evaluation for SWE. Appendix A.1 provides task counts and the selection procedure. Each coding condition is conﬁgured for three trials per model and task. VisualBench contains 18 visual and interactive tasks. Each provides task description and any supporting ﬁles, and asks the agent to produce an artifact, such as playable game, an interactive 3D conﬁgurator, or sales data explorer. For models without native visual capabilities, look_at tool renders the artifact and returns description from Qwen3.7-Plus. Raters from an internal company data team compare artifacts from veriﬁcation condition and the baseline for the same task and model, with conditions hidden and sides randomized. They receive the task brief and short interaction instructions, and judge functionality and visual quality against the task requirements. Outcomes are recorded as wins, losses, or ties; cases where both artifacts fail are recorded separately. We evaluate one representative design from each of L0L2 and four L3 designs, with two trials conﬁgured per task, model, and condition. Appendix provides the full descriptions of all 18 tasks, expert instructions, and screenshots of the evaluation interface. Environment. All experiments run in E2B cloud sandboxes (E2B, 2026), orchestrated with Harbor (Harbor Framework Team, 2026). Each trial starts in fresh sandbox containing the task ﬁles, dependencies, and execution tools. The agent interacts with this environment by reading and editing ﬁles, running commands, and inspecting outputs. sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: In this section, we analyze L0 initial instructions in Section 5.1, L1 execution-time reminders in Section 5.2, L2 completion gates in Section 5.3, and L3 independent review in Section 5.4.

sections.title: 5.1 L0: INITIAL INSTRUCTIONS
sections.content: L0 veriﬁcation instructions yield modest average coding gains, with substantial differences across models and benchmarks. Instructions with the system role improve accuracy by +3.3 points on TB and +3.9 points on SWE, compared with +1.2 and 1.1 points for instructions with the user role, as shown in Tables 2 and 3. On SWE, MiniMax-M2.5 beneﬁts from both variants (+12.6/ + 8.0 points for system/user), whereas Qwen3.8-Max declines under both (2.3/ 2.3). Qwen3.8-Max instead gains +8.0/ + 4.0 points on TB with the system/user roles. On VisualBench, L0 yields an average net preference of 3.2 points over the baseline, as shown in Figure 3. DeepSeek V4-Flash receives net preference of +5.6 points, while GLM-5.2 receives 8.3 points despite its positive accuracy gains on both coding benchmarks. Cost changes are modest: system/user instructions incur 1.08/1.03 baseline cost on TB and 0.94/0.93 on SWE, as shown in Figure 2. Average output tokens and agent turns remain close to or below baseline levels across both benchmarks and message roles, at 0.901.00 and 0.94 0.99, respectively, as reported in Appendix Table 6. These average gains are not accompanied by consistently increased generation or longer interactions. sections.title: 5.2 L1: EXECUTION-TIME REMINDERS
sections.content: Periodic and after-edit L1 reminders have similar average effects with the system message role: +3.8 versus +3.5 points on TB and +3.1 versus +3.6 on SWE. Switching the message role of after-edit reminders to user raises the average gain to +5.4 points on TB but lowers it to 0.3 on SWE, as shown in Tables 2 and 3. On VisualBench, MiniMax-M2.5 receives +12.5 points, while GLM-5.2 and Qwen3.7-Max each receive 12.5 points. Across the three L1 designs, average output tokens decrease by 1425% on TB and 710% on SWE, while cost ranges from 0.901.12 and 0.850.89 baseline, respectively, as shown in Figure 2 and Appendix Figure 15. Higher accuracy can also coexist with less generated output. On TB, Qwen3.7-Max gains +7.1/ + 14.3 points with after-edit system/user reminders while using 33%/28% fewer output tokens, respectively. On VisualBench, L1 yields an average net preference of 3.2 points over the baseline, as shown in Figure 3. Overall, we recommend veriﬁcation reminders after code edits to focus the agent on task requirements and the resulting artifact alongside the code itself. The average accuracy gains with fewer output tokens on TB and SWE support using L1, while the VisualBench results motivate checks that also cover rendered output and interactive behavior. 6 Figure 2: Mean accuracy versus mean cost relative to baseline (method IDs are in Tables 2 and 3). Trajectory analysis distinguishes continued execution from task-relevant veriﬁcation. On TB, 9097% of after-edit user reminders are followed by execution commands within two agent turns, as reported in Appendix Table 8. The checks themselves also differ in coverage. On nginx-request-logging, Qwen3.7-Max checks the Nginx conﬁguration, HTTP responses, and access log after reminder and passes, whereas the baseline stops with an unﬁnished plan, as shown in Appendix Figure 27. However, Kimi-K2.7-Code veriﬁes compilation while overlooking invalid word substitutions on overfull-hbox, and DeepSeek V4-Flash veriﬁes output equality yet misses the runtime criterion on query-optimize, as shown in Appendix Figure 28 and Appendix Figure 29. L1 Takeaways Use veriﬁcation reminders after code edits to guide the agent in checking both the code and the resulting artifact against task requirements. Include checks of rendered output and interactive behavior when relevant.

sections.title: 5.3 L2: COMPLETION GATES
sections.content: L2 yields limited gains relative to its cost, even when rejection and earlier intervention improve average accuracy. Automated Reject completion yields +4.0/ + 5.3 points on TB/SWE, compared with +0.7/ + 0.5 for Inspect changes and +2.6/ 0.5 for automated Run and check. Using the system role for Run and check raises the gains to +4.5/+1.5 points. Earlier triggering also improves both user rechecking and user rejection: rechecking rises from +4.1/ 0.3 to +4.8/ + 4.1 points, while rejection rises from +2.1/ + 4.1 to +6.0/ + 6.2 points, the largest average gains among the tested L2 designs, as shown in Tables 2 and 3. Across the rejection designs, cost reaches 1.601.76 baseline on TB and 1.481.56 on SWE. Early user rechecking achieves its gains at lower cost of 1.13/1.20 baseline, respectively, as shown in Figure 2. On VisualBench, early rechecking yields an average net preference of +2.7 points, as shown in Figure 3. GLM-5.2 receives +9.4 points, while DeepSeek V4-Flash receives 8.0 points. Overall, we recommend avoiding completion-time self-checking, as its gains are limited relative to the additional cost and reopening work does not consistently improve the ﬁnal artifact. The L2 cases illustrate both useful repair and invalid ﬁnal states. On TB, model-level medians range from 1219 additional steps after user rejection, compared with 46 after Inspect changes. Filechanging actions follow user rejection in 8696% of L2 runs in which user rejection is triggered, as reported in Appendix Table 9. On regex-log, MiniMax-M2.5 resumes after early user rejection 7 Figure 3: VisualBench win, tie, and loss results. and ﬁnds that its regex misses dates placed before the IP address. It removes this ordering assumption and passes grading, whereas the baseline retains it and fails, as shown in Appendix Figure 30. On git-multibranch, Kimi-K2.7-Code responds to an early recheck with deployment tests that commit and push test content to the served branches. It leaves that content in place and fails, whereas the passing baseline restores the required branch contents, as shown in Appendix Figure 31. These cases show why further execution alone is insufﬁcient: completion gate creates an opportunity for repair, but the agent must still identify the relevant defect and preserve valid ﬁnal artifact. L2 Takeaways Avoid completion-time self-checking. Asking the main agent to recheck its own work can improve accuracy, but the gains are limited relative to the additional cost.

sections.title: 5.4 L3: INDEPENDENT REVIEW
sections.content: L3 delivers consistent improvement across all four designs on TB and SWE at modest additional cost. The gains range from +5.99.5 points on TB and +3.96.6 on SWE, as shown in Tables 2 and 3. Cost, including critic review and agent revision, is 1.131.25 baseline on TB and 1.00 1.04 on SWE, as shown in Figure 2. Compared with the strongest L2 design, the strongest L3 design achieves larger gain on TB (+9.5 versus +6.0 points) and comparable gain on SWE (+6.6 versus +6.2), at lower cost on both benchmarks. On VisualBench, all four L3 designs receive positive net preference, ranging from +13.2 to +23.8 points and exceeding the evaluated L0L2 designs, as shown in Appendix Table 12. Changes-based review outperforms trajectory-based review both without required visual inspection (+21.2 versus +13.2 points) and with it (+23.8 versus +21.6 points). Required visual inspection improves net preference for both contexts, with larger increase for trajectory-based review. Both changes-based designs receive positive net preference for all seven models, while trajectory-based designs retain some negative model-level results. Across the three benchmarks, the full trajectory does not consistently improve outcomes, and trajectory-based designs incur 2943% higher critic cost on TB and SWE. Overall, we recommend task requirements and changes as the default context for separate, low-cost critic. The trajectories illustrate how independent review turns additional checks into concrete repairs. On regex-log, MiniMax-M2.5 tests its regex and declares completion, but the critic tests case with the date appearing before the IP address and exposes missed match. The agent then revises the regex and passes, whereas the baseline performs its own tests but still fails, as shown in Appendix Figure 32. On cobol-modernization, Qwen3.7-Maxs implementation passes its own checks for valid and invalid transactions. The critic tests an arithmetic underﬂow and ﬁnds that Python writes negative sign that COBOLs unsigned ﬁeld omits, breaking the required record format. The agent reproduces the discrepancy, repairs the numeric formatting, and passes the external grader; the baseline declares success after its own comparisons but fails grading, as shown in Appendix Figure 33. In both examples, the critic tests case that the agent overlooked and supplies an executable failure that guides revision. This illustrates how an independent checking perspective can address 8 Figure 4: Scaling independent review on TB through additional review rounds (depth) and critics (width), showing accuracy versus mean critic token use. gaps in the agents self-veriﬁcation. On cancel-async-tasks, GLM-5.2s critic conﬁrms that asynchronous cleanup remains incomplete after cancellation, but the run reaches its 45-minute limit without completed repair after review, as shown in Appendix Figure 34. Scaling review. Increasing review depth (successive review rounds) or width (independent critics) further improves average accuracy on TB. One critic and one round achieve 62.7% accuracy at 38.2k mean critic tokens, compared with 65.6% at 79.5k for two rounds and 64.4% at 69.7k for two critics. All larger settings outperform single review, reaching 66.1% with four rounds and 65.8% with four critics, as shown in Figure 4. Four critics improve average accuracy by 3.1 points over one critic at 1.33 total cost, including revisions. Scaling veriﬁcation through low-cost critics can limit repeated execution by the main agent. By consolidating independent feedback before revision, four critics approach four-round accuracy at 19% lower total cost, as shown in Appendix Figure 23. L3 Takeaways Use separate, low-cost critic to check the deliverable and guide agent revision. Scaling review through additional rounds or independent critics further improves average accuracy.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we systematically study veriﬁcation in agent harnesses, comparing 17 designs across four layers of the agent lifecycle and seven frontier coding models on TB and SWE, with evaluation on VisualBench. We examine when to intervene, who checks the work, and how feedback leads to revision. Initial instructions and reminders yield modest, model-dependent coding gains without substantially increasing average output token use. Completion gates can improve accuracy but may substantially increase cost. Independent review offers more favorable accuracycost tradeoff on TB and SWE. On VisualBench, its four designs achieve net preferences of 13.223.8 points over the baseline, exceeding the evaluated L0L2 designs. Additional rounds or critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for veriﬁcation design in agent harnesses and support independent review as practical axis of test-time scaling.

That number means the positions have to live and update on the GPU; if youre stepping million particles in JavaScript each frame youve already lost. three.min.js is in your working directory - ship it locally and use it, or go raw WebGL, your call. want the motion to look like ﬂuid, not like points on springs: curl-noise ﬂow ﬁeld that evolves over time so the ﬁeld itself drifts, with particles that have momentum and trail rather than snapping. The mouse should push into the ﬂow - attract by default, repel on key or control, with the inﬂuence falling off smoothly with distance instead of hard radius. Make it read as depth: particles further away smaller and dimmer, additive light where they pile up, colour that responds to speed or curl so the structure of the ﬂow is visible. Particles should recycle when they drift out rather than the ﬁeld emptying. Give me way to see its real - live particle count and framerate on screen. It must survive window resize without rebuilding the world from scratch. Deliver, in your working directory: index.html (plus the local three.min.js if you use it) - runs ofﬂine.

sections.content: Build me the hero scene company would put at the top of its product page for wireless headphone. It should look photographed, not rendered by default settings: studio setup with key, ﬁll and rim light, soft shadows on the ground, and materials that actually differ - brushed metal on the band, soft matte on the cushions, subtle sheen where the light grazes an edge. Give the frame considered composition rather than an object centred in grey. want to interact with it. Drag to orbit and wheel to zoom, with the motion damped so it glides to stop rather than halting. gentle idle animation when leave it alone, which yields the moment touch it. Colour variants that switch the materials with smooth transition, not snap. An exploded-view toggle that separates the parts along sensible axes and reassembles them, with the parts labelled while apart. And hotspots on the object can click to focus the camera on detail and read short note about it. Handle window resize, and keep it smooth. Deliver, in your working directory: index.html plus the local three.min.js it loads - runs ofﬂine.

sections.title: Task description
sections.content: Build me terminal dashboard in Python (rich and textual are available) for the service ﬂeet in stats.json in your working directory - something Id leave open on second monitor. want more than table: the ﬂeet listing with per-service status, but also sparklines showing each services recent trend, an overall health summary that makes the worst thing on the ﬂeet obvious at glance, and live log pane that keeps scrolling. Colour-code ok / warn / crit and make severity readable from across the room - crit service should catch my eye without reading the text. It should be real interface, not static frame: laid out in panes that use the terminals full width, updating continuously with values that move plausibly rather than jumping randomly, sorted so problems surface to the top. If service crosses into crit, that transition should be visible when it happens. Handle narrow terminal without the layout collapsing into garbage. Then record it running. Deliver, in your working directory: demo.cast (an asciinema recording of at least 30 seconds showing live updates and at least one status transition) and screen.svg (one exported frame).

For L0L2, we select one representative intervention per layer: the system veriﬁcation instruction, the after-edit user reminder, and the user recheck request with the 80% early trigger. These use the same intervention deﬁnitions as TB and SWE. For L3, we compare changes-based and trajectory-based review, each with and without required visual inspection. Each design is compared with the baseline for the same task and coding model. Review depth and width are studied separately on Terminal-Bench. Each task supplies description and any supporting ﬁles without reference implementation. Tasks run in an environment with Python, Chromium, and ffmpeg, with additional tools where required. Browser artifacts run ofﬂine, with bundled libraries only where the task permits them. Raters and brieﬁng. The raters are members of an internal company data team. Before rating, the interface presents brieﬁng explaining the studys purpose, the blinded comparison, the four response options, and worked example of applying the criteria. Consent, compensation, and ethics approval. The human evaluation received ethics approval. Raters provided informed consent and were compensated under their existing contracts with the company. Blinded comparison. Raters compare artifacts for the same task and model with veriﬁcation conditions hidden and sides randomized. The interface presents the original task brief, its judging criteria, and short set of task-speciﬁc interaction steps. Both artifacts can be inspected side by side or opened individually at full size. Raters interact with live artifacts where available and inspect delivered recordings or renders where appropriate. Instructions to raters. The rating interface gives the following guidance: 1. Read the original task brief before comparing the artifacts. Judge against what the task asks for, including its functional and visual requirements. 2. Follow the task-speciﬁc interaction checklist on both artifacts. Click, drag, type, or play as needed to check the requested behavior; use the full-size view when the side-by-side view is too small. For keyboard controls, ﬁrst click inside the artifact to give it focus. 3. Choose or when one artifact better satisﬁes the task. Choose tie when both work and you cannot distinguish their quality. Choose both fail only when neither makes meaningful attempt at the task, such as when both are blank, broken, or unrelated to the request. An artifact that works poorly does not by itself justify both fail. 4. If only one side produces usable deliverable, choose that side even if it is rough. If page appears blank, refresh it once before judging. Visual polish should not outweigh missing functionality unless visual quality is itself the tasks objective. 5. Optionally leave short comment explaining the deciding issue, especially when the two artifacts are difﬁcult to distinguish. Example interaction checklist. For Breakout game, raters move the paddle with the arrow keys, launch the ball, clear several bricks, and deliberately let the ball drop. These actions check paddle control, collisions, scoring, and the loss condition. The judgment follows the requested game behavior rather than screenshot alone. 48 C.3 EXPERT EVALUATION INTERFACE Figure 24 shows the English rating interface for the Blender desk-scene task, with rendered images and turntable videos available on both sides. Raters can expand the task brief and judging guidance, follow the task-speciﬁc instructions, and inspect the two artifacts side by side or at full size. Four response buttons record preference for or B, tie, or failure of both artifacts; an optional comment records the reason for the judgment. sections.title: E VERIFICATION INSTRUCTIONS AND EXECUTION RULES
sections.content: We reproduce the intervention templates and the rules that place them in the conversation. Prompt wording comes from the harness implementation; line wrapping and dash typography are normalized for typesetting. Braced ﬁelds such as {detail} are ﬁlled at runtime. The critic prompts are presented as an opening, strategy-speciﬁc ﬁrst step, and shared remainder, so the four complete prompts can be reconstructed without repeating identical text. E.1 L0: INITIAL INSTRUCTIONS The veriﬁcation instructions below are appended to the system prompt or the users initial task request. Veriﬁcation instructions When youre done, dont just re-read your work - actually run it. Run what you changed the way it really gets used (the command, route, or test someone would actually hit) and read the real output and exit code. If its something person looks at, render it and look at the result; if its interactive, exercise the core interactions and conﬁrm the state really changes - loading is not working. Re-reading the code and not spotting anything isnt evidence. Fix anything thats wrong. E.2 L1: EXECUTION-TIME REMINDERS Periodic reminders follow every third turn after the ﬁrst edit; after-edit reminders follow each edit. Both stop at four. After tool results, reminders with the system role include the marker below; those with the user role contain only the shared body.

sections.title: Marker for the system role
sections.content: [AUTOMATED SELF-VERIFY CHECKPOINT - not message from the user]

sections.title: Shared reminder body
sections.content: Youve made edits since you last ran anything. Before continuing - or calling it done - RUN what you changed at its real surface (the command / route / CLI its user or test hits) and read the actual output and exit code - or, if its something user LOOKS AT (a page, chart, UI), RENDER it and look at the actual result; if its INTERACTIVE, also EXERCISE its core interactions (keys / clicks) and conﬁrm the state changes - loading is not functioning. Re-reading the code, or ﬁnding nothing wrong, is NOT evidence; if you genuinely cant run it here, say unveriﬁed rather than claiming its done. Fix what breaks now, while its fresh. E.3 L2: COMPLETION GATES turn without tool call triggers the gate. Each single-pass condition sends one message and accepts the next stop. The automated designs use the user message role with the name system-reminder; the System design of Run and check uses the system message role. The User designs use the user message role without this marker. Early-trigger variants also ﬁre at the next turn boundary after 80% of the tasks time limit if the agent has not stopped. Inspect changes (automated) [FINAL REVIEW - not message from the user] Before you ﬁnish: re-read every change you made and look it over carefully for mistakes, missed requirements, or edge cases. If you spot anything wrong, ﬁx it now; otherwise you may ﬁnish. Run and check (automated or system) [FINAL CHECK - not message from the user] Before you ﬁnish: RUN what you changed at its real surface (the command / route / CLI its user or test hits) and read the actual output and exit code - or, if its something user LOOKS AT (a page, chart, UI), RENDER it and look at the actual result; if its INTERACTIVE, also EXERCISE its core interactions (keys / clicks) and conﬁrm the state changes - 62 loading is not functioning. Re-reading the code, or ﬁnding nothing wrong, is NOT evidence; if you genuinely cant run it here, say unveriﬁed rather than claiming its done. Fix anything that breaks; only then ﬁnish. Recheck before ﬁnishing (user) Before we call this done - please double-check your work by actually running it, not by re-reading it. Run what you changed the way it really gets used (the command, route, or test someone would actually hit) and read the real output and exit code. If its something person looks at, render it and look at the result; if its interactive, exercise the core interactions and conﬁrm the state really changes - loading is not working. Re-reading the code and not spotting anything isnt evidence. Fix anything thats wrong. Reject completion (automated) [AUTOMATED VERIFICATION - not message from the user] An automated veriﬁcation pass has determined this task is NOT complete. Keep working; do not ﬁnish yet. Reject completion (user) An automated veriﬁcation pass has determined this task is NOT complete. Keep working; do not ﬁnish yet. E.4 L3: INDEPENDENT REVIEW The critic receives the review instructions in system message. separate user message contains the task and changes; trajectory conditions also include the agents reasoning, messages, and actions. Each critic starts in fresh context and can inspect the live sandbox. The standard single-pass design ends on approval; an objection returns ﬁndings to the agent, whose next delivery is accepted without another review. Prompt assembly. Choose the opening for the designs strategy and context, append Work in THREE steps:, then the matching ﬁrst step and the shared steps below. The common remainder includes the non-mutation rule and the JSON output format. Task-ﬁrst opening: changes You are CRITIC auditing an agents completed work - INDEPENDENTLY and skeptically, against the task spec alone. You are given the agents changes (git diff) and its live sandbox; you have shell access. The decisive failure is usually NOT visible in what the agent already ran or in clean read of the diff - form your OWN judgment by RUNNING the real deliverable. Task-ﬁrst opening: trajectory You are CRITIC auditing an agents completed work - INDEPENDENTLY and skeptically. The agents full session is provided: what it built, where, and how. Do NOT trust its reasoning or that its commands passed; the decisive failure is usually NOT in what it already ran - form your OWN judgment by RUNNING the real deliverable. Claim-guided opening: changes You are CRITIC auditing an agents completed work against the task spec. You are given the agents changes (git diff) and its live sandbox; you have shell access. READ the diff carefully - it is your MAP of the audit: where the agent worked, what it believes it did, and what it left untouched. It tells you WHERE to look, never what is TRUE: every claim in or around it is the agents hypothesis, and your job is to try to FALSIFY each one by running the real deliverable. Claim-guided opening: trajectory You are CRITIC auditing an agents completed work against the task spec. The agents full session is provided: what it built, where, how - and what it TOLD ITSELF along the way. READ it critically: the session is your MAP of the audit - where the agent worked, which checks it actually ran, where it 63 asserted success without one, where it resolved ambiguity by interpretation. It tells you WHERE to look and what the agent BELIEVES, never what is TRUE: every claim in it is the agents hypothesis, and your job is to try to FALSIFY each one by running the real deliverable. Task-ﬁrst step 1 1. CHECKLIST - enumerate the tasks real requirements as WEIGHTED list (3=core, 2=important, 1=nice-to-have), covering EVERY one. Above all, name the deep correctness property the task hinges on - WHERE would passing-LOOKING solution still be wrong? - and put weight-3 item there. Claim-guided step 1 1. CHECKLIST FROM CRITICAL READING - read the evidence FIRST, adversarially, before touching the sandbox: - THE SPEC: enumerate the tasks real requirements as WEIGHTED list (3=core, 2=important, 1=nice-to-have), covering EVERY one. Name the deep correctness property the task hinges on - WHERE would passing-LOOKING solution still be wrong? - and put weight-3 item there. - THE CHANGE, hunk by hunk: for each change ask what it ASSUMES, what it could BREAK, and whether it matches the specs letter; then ask what the spec requires that NO hunk touches - an omitted change is itself likely bug. Changes are where bugs live; audit coverage follows the change surface. - THE AGENTS OWN WORDS (its session, commit messages, comments), decision by decision: mark every point where it asserts success (tested, works, done), skips check, or resolves an ambiguity by interpretation. Each such CLAIM becomes checklist item. claim is hypothesis the agent asserts - NEVER carry one forward as fact; your job is to falsify or conﬁrm each by observation. The agent believing it is done is not evidence that it is. Shared steps 23 and verdict format 2. VERIFY BY RUNNING (observation, not reading) - for EACH item, probe the ACTUAL deliverable and ground your claim ONLY in the output you observe: - RUN it through the REAL surface its user/test hits - the actual command, route, CLI, or UI (build it, hit the route, render it, run the projects own tests); watch the ACTUAL result. For anything user looks at, the evidence is the RENDERED result you saw; if its interactive, loading != functioning - exercise it (send input / submit / click) and conﬁrm an observed state change. - RECOMPUTE the expected answer INDEPENDENTLY from the spec/ground truth. Do NOT re-derive it the agents way, import-and-call its internals, or re-implement the logic - that proves YOUR call, not the deliverable; and green test suite alone can pass proxy. You MAY write + run THROWAWAY probes under /tmp (never in the workspace). - clean read settles nothing - looked and saw nothing wrong is absence of disproof, not proof. If probe errors or is inconclusive, FIX it and RE-RUN; check that didnt run proves nothing. No runtime surface (pure data/conﬁg/docs) -> check real content vs the spec. Genuinely CANT run the decisive check (missing tool/service/cred, wont build) -> report unveriﬁed: <what & why>, never assume it works. 3. VERDICT - judge HOLISTICALLY, ONLY from evidence you observed; `done`=true ONLY when probe you RAN positively DEMONSTRATES the requirement holds. Be strict, no beneﬁt of the doubt. It is NOT done if probe was inconclusive, the requirement is ambiguous and the agent may have taken the wrong interpretation (an OMITTED expected step is itself likely bug, not an acceptable default), or you cant tell which of several plausible answers is right. Probably ﬁne is not conﬁrmation. Distrust your OWN pass too - before marking anything met, rule out two traps: PROXY (a weaker check wrong answer could also pass - it merely ran / has the right shape / derived property, not the exact required RESULT) and SHARED MISTAKE (you repeated the agents own error). Cant rule either out -> NOT conﬁrmed. NEVER MUTATE THE DELIVERABLE - you OBSERVE, never change it: no modify/move/delete/rename/regenerate/reset, no `sed -i`, no `>` into its ﬁles, no rm, no git add/commit (that destroys what youre judging and INVALIDATES the verdict). Found problem? REPORT it, dont repair it. Throwaway probes go in /tmp. Judge ONLY the tasks own requirements; never hunt for hidden grading tests. Common blind spots: history/backups/logs the visible artifact hides, boundary inputs, met-in-display-but-not-storage, one of several targets silently skipped, value that looks plausible but was never checked vs ground truth. When youve probed EVERY requirement, STOP calling tools and output ONLY this JSON on that ﬁnal turn - `feedback` goes to the agent verbatim (the concrete gap + how to resolve it: what the output showed vs what the requirement needs - dont tell it to rewrite working code): {"done": false, "feedback": "...", "checklist": [{"requirement": "...", "met": false, "evidence": "<the probe you RAN + what it showed>"}]} 64 Feedback after review. The agent receives an objection as user message using the template below. The detail ﬁeld contains unmet requirements and, where available, the critics feedback.

sections.title: Feedback after an objection
sections.content: A strict veriﬁcation pass determined the task is NOT yet complete. Unmet requirements / defects: {detail} Address these, then stop again only when the task is truly complete. Required visual inspection on VisualBench. The visual review conditions use the Claim-guided strategy with Changes or Trajectory context. Required-inspection variants enable the critics viewing tool and append the following two clauses; the second accompanies temporal capture support.

sections.title: Required visual inspection
sections.content: MANDATORY - LOOK AT THE ARTIFACT: for ANY deliverable user perceives (a page, UI, game, chart, SVG, animation, PDF, image, or audio), you MUST use the `view` tool: render it to screenshot(s) (or load the media) and judge what you actually SAW or HEARD, citing it in that items `evidence` (what was on screen, not what the source says). If it is INTERACTIVE, drive it - `click` / `scroll_to` / `serve` running app - and view it AGAIN after the interaction; one pre-interaction screenshot is not veriﬁcation of behavior. verdict on perceptual requirement without viewed render is INVALID: mark that item unveriﬁed: not viewed, never met.

sections.title: Temporal inspection for moving artifacts
sections.content: For anything that MOVES on its own (animation, simulation, living scene, cycling effect): one screenshot proves NOTHING - capture it at TWO well-separated moments (`view` with wait_for=2000, then wait_for=15000) and compare. DIFFERENT frames = the motion is real; IDENTICAL frames = the world is frozen and the requirement is NOT met, no matter how good the still looks. E.5 REVIEW DEPTH AND WIDTH The TB scaling sweep uses claim-guided review with changes. Depth allows up to critic rounds, subject to the remaining budget. Subsequent rounds receive the critics prior checklist and feedback. Review width. Width uses critics with separate contexts on the same delivery. The implementation runs the reviews sequentially in the shared sandbox; critics do not receive one anothers assessments. Any returned objection sends the work back to the agent, with dissenting ﬁndings grouped by critic. Acceptance requires no returned objection. The width sweep uses one panel round, so an agents subsequent revision is not reviewed again. E.5.1 PROMPTS FOR ADDITIONAL REVIEW ROUNDS Prior-review context for subsequent critic rounds YOUR PREVIOUS AUDIT of this same deliverable (round {n} - verdict: {verdict}): {checklist} Feedback you gave: {feedback} HOW TO USE IT - it is your COVERAGE MAP, not your conclusion; your previous verdict carries NO authority this round, only what you now observe does: 1. FIRST re-derive the requirement checklist from the TASK above, from scratch. Compare it to your previous checklist: any requirement the old list MISSED or misread is your primary suspect - probe it ﬁrst.

sections.title: Continuation after an objection
sections.content: 2. The agent has since reworked. For each previously-FAILED item, re-run the decisive probe against the CURRENT state - the agent says it ﬁxed it proves nothing. 3. Rework breaks things: spot-check the highest-weight previously-MET items for regressions.
